A Canberra dinner party. A host’s plan to kill her boyfriend. Guests who went along with the whole thing.
Thirty years on, one question remains; why did nobody stop her? Even the killer can’t answer it.

Anu Singh, a gifted law student at the Australian National University, is one of Australia’s most notorious femme fatales.
What the 25-year-old did one warm ‘90s weekend to Joe Cinque, the man she appeared to love, defies all logic.
Both because of the chilling nature in which she carried out his killing and the reaction of her dearest friends who, once told of her plan, did not try to intervene.

‘Must have been aware … he was in danger’
On October 21, 1997, Anu Singh, a “happy-go-lucky” 25-year-old student at Canberra’s largest university was in the final stages of a plan to poison her 26-year-old civil engineer boyfriend and the man she shared an apartment with in the inner-north suburb of Downer.

It is at that same apartment where, the night prior, Singh hosted one of her now notorious dinner parties and spoke openly about her desire to end her boyfriend’s life. A suicide pact of sorts that was sadly one-sided.

None of the guests that night took the threat seriously, but before the night was out, Cinque was unconscious.
One of Singh’s friends, Madhavi Rao, had begun to realise that the disturbing conversations she was having with the daughter of two Sydney doctors might be genuine. But she did not confront her friend, or try to stop her.
Instead, according to court documents seen by news.com.au, Rao “kne

Judge Ken Crispin wrote that the “facts do not prove Rao shared Ms Singh’s criminal purpose or that she aided and abetted her”.
“She may have been interceding with Ms Singh with a view to persuading her to change her mind or she may have failed to intervene because she could not face Ms Singh or did not know what to do,” he wrote.
“She may have simply hoped that Ms Singh would have a change of hea

regions.text: Convicted killer Anu Singh with her father, Doctor Paddy Singh, leaving the ACT Supreme Court in Canberra, after she was released on parole.

Five days later, on October 26, Singh, Cinque and Rao hosted guests for a second dinner that week.
Singh had told friends at the first dinner that a terrible crime would be committed at the second dinner. How they perceived her comments remains a mystery, but we know now that Singh was deadly serious.

It did not happen quickly.
Over 36 hours, Cinque vomited blood and turned blue. Singh kept watching, but did not intervene.

She instead left the couple’s home between 5am and 6am, several hours after administering the lethal dose, but returned at midday in a panic. Cinque was still alive.
Frantic, she phoned a friend and confessed. That friend urged her to call an ambulance immediately, but Singh replied: “It’s too late, he’s gone anyway.”
“Look, Anu, if you call paramedics, you will have an angry boyfriend when he wak

Thirty-six hours after Singh drugged her boyfriend, she called Triple-Zero. It took 20 minutes for her to provide them with the correct address.
Singh: Could I get an ambulance please? I have a person potentially overdosed on heroin.

000: Potentially overdosed?
Singh: Well, he’s not — he’s vomiting everywhere, blood stuff.

000: He’s vomiting blood? Right, okay, what’s the address?
Singh: Is that a bad sign?
000: What’s the address?
Singh: Can you hang on, please just tell me, is that a bad sign?

000: That’s — well it’s not good if he’s vomiting blood.
Singh: Oh, is he going to be okay?
000: I don’t know, I’ll send an ambulance for them to check him out.

Singh: Fair enough.
Asked for her name, Anu Singh replied: “Oh, oh God, Olivia. Olivia, Olivia, oh f***, hang on, hang on.”

When paramedics did finally arrive, it was too late.
Author Helen Garner, who wrote the book Joe Cinque’s Consolation after attending Singh’s trial, pondered: “Did Joe Cinque have his wits about him long enough to grasp what was going on? Anu Singh must know, but she wasn’t talking.”

‘A ghoulish game with Joe the unsuspecting sacrifice’
Tonia Liosatos was in the courtroom when Joe’s mother Maria Cinque screamed at Singh: “You’re a witch.”

The insult was not a throwaway line, it was meant literally.
“That was the feeling in the courtroom, that Anu had put a spell over all these people,” Liosatos told news.com.au this week.
“Even now I’m shaking my head just thinking, how did that happen?”
The former Canberra court reporter who worked at the ABC and The Canberra Times, was front and centre when the case became a national spectacle.

Joe Cinque never saw it coming.

“The sentence was a joke and an insult to the Cinques,” she told news.com.au. “It was 10 (years) on the top, she was out in four (years) and doing the interview circuit.”
The journalist listened in court as the Triple-Zero call was played out.
“There was this phone call that we heard — the court reporters — it was seemingly so bizarre.
“It was absolutely chaotic and frustrating. We know now what h

Her impression is that Cinque never saw it coming.
“He was so unaware of what she was capable of. She must’ve presented such a charming persona to Joe who was really quite obviously naive. But you would be naive; nobody thinks their partner is planning their death.

“The cold, calculating nature of it was just so confronting.”
She says she covered a number of high-profile murders but none had the impact on her that Singh’s case did.

“Leading up to Joe’s death it was all about Anu. In court it was all about Anu. And then when she got out it was all about Anu. I couldn’t bear it and it was so hard for the Cinques to have to deal with it.
“The impression of Anu was — I can see her in my mind in court. She had some kind of aura that it was all about her. She was striking, but in a way because we knew it had happened, I felt some

‘She believed … animals were crawling beneath her skin’
Ten years ago, Ginger Gorman convinced Singh to meet her in suburban Sydney. It took some wrangling — the killer was initially very resistant.

When they met, Singh sat across from Gorman on an outside table at a coffee shop.
Singh had finished her law degree and obtained a master’s degree in criminology. In 2012, the daughter of two Indian doctors completed her 100,000-word PhD thesis on understanding female criminality in Australia.
She was the picture of a free woman, at least on the outside.
During their chat, one you can listen to in

“What I did was a horrible thing,” Singh told Gorman.
Asked why she killed Cinque, Singh replied, “There’s no rational motivation at all. I was mentally unwell, and I still grapple with that. I still grapple with the whys.

Speaking to news.com.au this week, the award-winning social justice journalist and author said she still replays one part of the conversation in her head.
“The question I asked her very directly: ‘why did you kill Joe?’ Her answer was essentially that she didn’t know. She said there was no rational motivation and that she still couldn’t understand it herself.
“After everything written and said abo

images.alt: Killer Anu Singh holds her thesis, titled Offending Women. Picture: Ginger Gorman

regions.text: Killer Anu Singh holds her thesis, titled Offending Women. Picture: Ginger Gorman

Gorman lived close to where Cinque was killed in Canberra and once owned an apartment on the same street. So it hit home extra hard when it happened.
She read books about the case but wanted to hear Singh’s account directly. When they did meet, her thoughts about the crime changed.
“Nothing excuses killing another human being, and Anu herself took responsibility when I interviewed her,” Gorman tol

images.alt: Anu Singh, pictured in a Sydney park in December 2015. Picture: Ginger Gorman

regions.text: Anu Singh, pictured in a Sydney park in December 2015. Picture: Ginger Gorman

“One of the psychiatrists mentioned a state of disassociation, perhaps, like disassociated from reality. I don’t know. There’s no rational explanation,” she said in their 2016 interview.
“If I could turn back that clock. If I could have listened to people back then, and gotten the right sort of help, then this wouldn’t have happened.
“That’s obviously something I live with, and I can’t turn back t

Maria Cinque told Gorman it will never happen.
“You tell that. For Anu to not come near me. She’s a monster. She’s selfish, she doesn’t think about anybody else. Feel sorry? I don’t believe that. She doesn’t.

“She’s sorry just because of what happened to her, not because of what she did to my son.”
Gorman has other unanswered questions, those created by Cinque’s absence.
“Who would he be now? What sort of life would he have had? What were the ordinary and extraordinary things he would have done?

images.alt: Maggie Naouri as Anu Singh behind Jerome Meyer as Joe Cinque in the film Joe Cinque's Consolation. Picture: Supplied

regions.text: Maggie Naouri as Anu Singh behind Jerome Meyer as Joe Cinque in the film Joe Cinque's Consolation. Picture: Supplied

“Everyone else connected with this story has had nearly 30 years to grow older, change and tell their version of events. Joe didn’t get that chance. That’s the part I find unbearably sad.”
Helen Garner was in the ACT courtroom when Singh learned her fate. Later, she penned the award-winning book that was then turned into a film.

News.com.au contacted Garner for this story. She said she is “happy to step back and allow others to speak on this sad anniversary”.
Anu Singh could not be reached for comment.
